chapter: Hollywood life and the musicians' union
title: Restrictive covenant suits over his Hollywood houses
summary: Neighbors sued over his purchase; he won, and later stalled until the Supreme Court made covenants unenforceable.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Right. Then on some of these non-musical matters, you were then -- had some difficulty about the house. Some neighbors in the mid forties, perhaps just around the end of World War II, brought suit against you or something.
Yes.

... because they felt that black people were not to be in that neighborhood. There was a restrictive covenant which your purchase of the house violated, and they wanted ... they brought -- did they bring suit? I mean how did they actually ...
Yes. They actually brought suit against us.
Against you or against the seller; the people that sold it to you, or ...
No, they ... I don't remember whether
they brought it against the people who sold it -- I don't think so. They were long gone, you know.
Yeah.
They couldn't have cared less, but they certainly brought it against me and the then Mrs. Carter.
Right.
And then, you know, we decided to fight the suit, and we won it.
Right. That was a period in which, wasn't it -- that the restrictive covenants were declared to be unenforceable.

No, not yet. That was in 1945. What happened in this particular suit was that by virtue of the neighborhood already taking on a different character, you know, I think that had something to do with our winning the suit.
But the other one was the house that I bought subsequent to that.
This was another suit?
Yes, but it never developed into a suit. Actually, I just had some letters from the attorney who was working for the neighborhood association or something.
Right.
Didn't think I should be there, and all I did, I ... he was quite decent about it -- as decent

as I consider him, under the circumstances -- and we went back and forth. I told him, well, I didn't really like the area anyway, and I had decided to sell -- but if he wanted to sue me, you know, they could certainly do so. But I thought we both saved a lot of money in litigation, if they waited.

Of course I knew at this time that there was pending this case about the restrictive convenants, you know, and while I was stalling, that came to a head with the announcement that I guess, the United States Supreme Court had declared the restrictive convenants unenforceable, so that sort of left me off the hook and they let me alone.
Right. That was the second house.
That was the second house.
Well, where was that first house?

The first house, I think was on ... where was it? Gee, there were a couple of houses. I think there was one on Kenwood or something --- I'm not sure, as a matter of fact, for some reason I guess I'd rather forget that house. I only lived in that house for about 2 weeks. With myself.
Uh huh. And the second one was the one that ...
The second was on Hollyridge Drive in Hollywood, where I lived for 18 years.
Right. That was the one that you
That was the one that I said I was going to sell.
Oh, but you didn't.
Of course. I had no intention of selling, but I was just stalling for time to keep from spending money on legal fees and going in to Court for all of that, and ...
When this whole question would become, as the lawyers say, 'moot' with the Supreme Court decision.
Yes, that's right exactly.
